headline: THE LEAGUE OF LEGENDS WORLD FINAL LOST 41 PERCENT OF ITS PEAK AUDIENCE ON SATURDAY AND ITS HOURS WATCHED BARELY MOVED, BECAUSE THE BROADCAST RAN ROUGHLY 18 HOURS LONGER, AND ONE CO-STREAMER'S PEAK WAS 40 PERCENT THE SIZE OF TWITCH'S ENTIRE PLATFORM PEAK
deck: Here is the clearest demonstration this year of why hours watched is not an audience.  Nearly three million fewer people watched the League of Legends final at the same time as last year.  The hours figure went nowhere, because the event simply stayed on air longer.  And the audience that did show up was not where the sponsor bought.
tldr: The League of Legends world final peaked at about 3.98 million people watching at once on Saturday, down 41 percent on last year, while its hours watched stayed flat at over 130 million because the broadcast ran about 107 hours against under 89 last year, and at the Streamer Awards around 77 percent of hours watched happened on community and co-stream channels rather than the official feed.  Ask every live seller for peak concurrents, average concurrents and total airtime before you price anything, and get the co-stream split in writing so you can judge how much of the event you are actually buying.

Twitch says four times as many creators landed a brand sponsorship this year while the money going out only doubled, which means the average sponsored creator is being paid roughly half what they were, and the supply came from platform matchmaking rather than from demand falling away.  Get a quote this week for four to six mid-sized live creators instead of one large one, and build the assets phone-first, because about half of Twitch's monthly viewers and more than 70 percent of its new viewers are on a phone.

An IAB report carrying Similarweb data found people who get a brand recommended by an AI assistant are 2.5 times more likely to visit that brand's site within seven days, but only 8.8 percent of those visits are credited to the AI, with 55.9 percent going to search and 19.9 percent to direct, which is the same hole that has always swallowed creator video.  Add one measure to your next campaign that the last click cannot steal, such as weekly branded search volume or a landing page that exists only inside the creator's video.

A single sponsored post from a mid-tier lifestyle creator now starts at 8,000 to 10,000 dollars while a multi-episode series runs well into five figures and reaches six with usage rights and category exclusivity, and Anthropologie's global chief executive judges its series on earned reach and non-follower reach first, with sales only after the whole run has finished.  Agree the scorecard before the fee on anything episodic, put non-follower reach at the top of it, and take engagement rate off the sheet entirely.

Live shopping in America is heading for nearly 20 billion dollars this year with spend per buyer up 23 percent to 339.27 dollars, and Adobe found people are nearly 70 percent more likely to buy during a livestream when they can see other people bidding, which is why one seller doing over 200,000 dollars a month says he hates auctions and runs two hours of them daily anyway.  Put a mechanic in every stream that makes other people's demand visible on screen, place it at the end rather than the start, and split your stream into service, normal-price selling and competition in that order.

A 240,000 subscriber British electronics repair channel roughly doubled its median views, from 108,045 to 214,475, by switching from repairing toys to repairing equipment people earn a living with, and its three best performers after the top one are the only three videos that name a tool manufacturer in the title, while its single biggest video of the last six months is still a toy.  Measure the median of your own channel's last ten videos against the ten before and manage the floor, because a sponsor buys the typical video rather than the one that spiked.

TikTok Live is being reported as holding 14 percent of game streaming, level with Kick, on 2.5 billion hours watched and 96 percent growth, with no peak or average concurrent figure anywhere in the report and no published numbers that let anybody work one out.  When a platform pitches you a share of market, establish straight away whether it is a share of hours or a share of simultaneous audience, and ask for the average concurrents of the specific streams you would be buying.
